name: Between the Sheets
subject: Sex
tagline: Twenty questions on the birds, the bees and the science, history and strange animal facts of sex. Grown-ups only. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: Which hormone, released during orgasm, cuddling and breastfeeding, is nicknamed the 'love hormone'?
questions.w: Oxytocin, made in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary gland.
questions.more: Oxytocin also triggers contractions in labour and the let-down of milk, which is why a synthetic version is used to induce births. Studies in prairie voles, one of the few mammals that pair for life, found that blocking oxytocin stops the animals from bonding with a mate.

questions.q: Which part of the human body is the only organ known to exist purely for pleasure?
questions.w: The clitoris, which has no other known job.
questions.more: Most of the clitoris is internal: the visible glans is the tip of a wishbone-shaped organ about nine centimetres long. Its full anatomy was not properly mapped until urologist Helen O'Connell published dissections in 1998, a year after the same journal ran a detailed paper on the penis.

questions.q: A full-term human pregnancy is counted as about how many weeks from the first day of the last period?
questions.w: 40 weeks, or nine months and a bit.
questions.more: The count starts about two weeks before conception even happens, because the last period is the one date most people know. Only about four per cent of babies arrive on their due date; 'full term' is now defined as 39 to 40 weeks and six days.

questions.q: The word 'aphrodisiac' is named after the Greek goddess of what?
questions.w: Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty, whose Roman counterpart is Venus.
questions.more: Aphrodite was said to have been born from sea foam, which is why so many supposed aphrodisiacs are seafood: oysters, above all. No food has ever been shown to work as one in a proper trial, though oysters do contain a lot of zinc, which the body needs to make testosterone.

questions.q: Which great ape is famous for using sex to settle arguments and keep the peace in its groups?
questions.w: The bonobo, our closest living relative alongside the chimpanzee.
questions.more: Bonobo groups are led by females, and sexual contact between almost any pair of adults defuses tension over food or newcomers. They live only south of the Congo River; chimpanzees, which live north of it, sort out the same disputes with violence.

questions.q: The birth-control pill was first approved for contraception in the United States in which decade?
questions.w: 1960: the Food and Drug Administration approved Enovid in May of that year.
questions.more: Enovid had been on sale since 1957, officially for menstrual disorders, and an unusual number of women suddenly reported those. Within five years more than six million American women were on the pill, though several states still banned contraception for unmarried women until 1972.

questions.q: True or false: in seahorses, it is the male that becomes pregnant and gives birth.
questions.w: True. The female deposits her eggs in the male's pouch, where he fertilises and carries them.
questions.more: The male seahorse's brood pouch does real pregnancy work: it controls salt levels, supplies oxygen and nutrients, and even shares genes with the placenta of mammals. Labour can last hours and release well over a thousand tiny seahorses, none of which get any further parenting.

questions.q: Viagra was originally developed and tested as a treatment for what?
questions.w: Angina: Pfizer's scientists were trying to widen blood vessels around the heart.
questions.more: The trials in Wales in the early 1990s were a flop for the heart, but male volunteers kept reporting a notable side effect and were reluctant to hand back their leftover pills. Sildenafil was approved for erectile dysfunction in March 1998 and sold more than a billion dollars' worth in its first year.

questions.q: After sperm are made in the testes, in which coiled tube do they mature and wait?
questions.w: The epididymis, which sits on the back of each testicle.
questions.more: Uncoiled, each epididymis would be about six metres long, and sperm take around two weeks to travel through it and learn to swim. A vasectomy cuts the vas deferens, the next tube along, which is why the testes keep making sperm that are simply reabsorbed.

questions.q: Put the four stages of Masters and Johnson's human sexual response cycle in order.
questions.w: Excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution, as set out in Human Sexual Response in 1966.
questions.more: William Masters and Virginia Johnson watched and wired up hundreds of volunteers in their St Louis laboratory over eleven years, something no scientist had done before. The four-stage model has since been criticised for leaving out desire, which Helen Singer Kaplan added in the 1970s.

questions.q: Which was the first country in the world to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2001?
questions.w: The Netherlands, where the first four couples married in Amsterdam just after midnight on 1 April 2001.
questions.more: Denmark had been first with registered partnerships in 1989, but full marriage waited for the Dutch law. Belgium followed in 2003, then Spain and Canada in 2005. By 2026 more than three dozen countries had followed.

questions.q: The Kama Sutra, the ancient Indian text on love and pleasure, was written in which language?
questions.w: Sanskrit, by the sage Vatsyayana, probably in the third century.
questions.more: Only one of its seven books is about sexual positions. The rest cover courtship, marriage, running a household, and how to behave as a courtesan or a wife. The Victorian explorer Richard Burton published the first English translation in 1883, privately, to dodge the obscenity laws.

questions.q: The vaccine Gardasil protects against which sexually transmitted infection, the most common one in the world?
questions.w: HPV, which causes almost all cervical cancers as well as genital warts.
questions.more: Most sexually active people catch HPV at some point and clear it without noticing. The vaccine, introduced in 2006, has cut cervical cancer in vaccinated women by close to 90 per cent in British and Swedish studies, and Australia expects to eliminate the disease within a generation.

questions.q: Most male mammals have a penis bone, called the baculum. Which of these does not?
questions.w: Humans. Walruses have the biggest of all, up to 60 centimetres long.
questions.more: Chimpanzees and gorillas keep a tiny baculum, so humans lost theirs somewhere in the last few million years. One theory links the loss to shorter mating times in pair-bonded species. Native Alaskans carve walrus bacula into tools and handles, known as oosiks.

questions.q: The Kinsey Institute, founded by the sex researcher Alfred Kinsey in 1947, is part of which university?
questions.w: Indiana University in Bloomington, where Kinsey taught zoology.
questions.more: Kinsey was a world authority on gall wasps before students' questions in a 1938 marriage course pushed him into sex research. His 1948 and 1953 reports, built on 18,000 interviews, sold hundreds of thousands of copies and introduced the 0-to-6 Kinsey scale of sexual orientation.

questions.q: The Comstock Act, passed by the US Congress in 1873, made it a crime to send what through the mail?
questions.w: Contraceptives, abortion drugs and any 'obscene' material, which the courts read to include birth-control advice.
questions.more: Anthony Comstock, a postal inspector and anti-vice crusader, boasted of destroying 160 tons of literature. The law was chipped away by court rulings from the 1930s but never fully repealed, and parts of it were cited again in abortion-pill litigation in the 2020s.

questions.q: Relative to its body size, which creature has the longest penis in the animal kingdom?
questions.w: The barnacle, whose penis can stretch to eight times its body length.
questions.more: Barnacles are glued to rocks for life, so they need the reach to find a neighbour. The blue whale has the longest in absolute terms, around three metres. The Argentine lake duck holds the bird record, with a corkscrew organ as long as its own body.

questions.q: In 1916 Margaret Sanger opened the first birth-control clinic in the United States. Where was it?
questions.w: Brownsville, Brooklyn, on 16 October 1916. Police shut it down after ten days.
questions.more: Sanger, a nurse, had watched women die from botched abortions on the Lower East Side. She served thirty days in a workhouse for the clinic, but her appeal won doctors the right to prescribe contraception in New York. The organisation she founded became Planned Parenthood in 1942.

questions.q: A surge of which hormone, roughly halfway through the menstrual cycle, triggers ovulation?
questions.w: Luteinising hormone, or LH, which peaks about 24 to 36 hours before the egg is released.
questions.more: Home ovulation tests work by detecting that LH surge in urine. After ovulation the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which pumps out progesterone to prepare the womb lining. The pill works largely by keeping hormone levels steady so the surge never comes.

questions.q: Which of these sexually transmitted infections are caused by bacteria and can be cured with antibiotics? Select all that apply.
questions.w: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis. Herpes and HIV are viruses, which antibiotics cannot touch.
questions.more: Syphilis was the first to fall, when penicillin was shown to cure it in 1943. Gonorrhoea is now the worry: strains resistant to almost every antibiotic have appeared, and the World Health Organization lists it as a priority threat. Chlamydia usually has no symptoms, which is why it is the most reported bacterial infection of all.
